claimVerdicts.note: Abstract p.1 gives 42 players and SNR = weekly CV% / test CV%. The Subjects section says 45, and the claim correctly flags the abstract figure.
Introduction p.1 defines signal and noise and says meaningful changes are 'those that exceed the "noise" in the test'.
CMJ methods p.3 match: 72 h postmatch, afternoon after the main skills session, self-chosen depth, retest 5 minutes apart, 50% warm-up then 3 maximal reps.
Abstract results are quoted accurately, and the claim correctly says the ranges cover all tools, not just CMJ.
Discussion p.5 says this, with the authors' own hedge 'may be the most responsive' kept, and limits it to professional AF.

Accurate attribution of the authors' citation of ref 24 and their hedged explanation ('may be explained by'). Note that the source's own CVs (2.1-3.5%) are not clearly higher than 2.7-4.3%, but the claim reports what the authors say.
Collings p.9 gives SEM = total SD x sqrt(1 - ICC).
Collings p.9 gives MDC = 1.96 x sqrt(2) x SEM, using a 95% CI for a change beyond 0.
Collings p.5 states this, citing ref 17, and the claim attributes it correctly.
Collings p.14 says this, keeping the hedges ('may all impact', 'may help improve').
Harper Table 1 (p.7) gives CV% 2.9/2.9/4.3 with flight-time jump height, and 27 male university team-sport athletes. The claim correctly notes that how the CV was derived is not described.
Garrett p.10: 'based on the 8% coefficient of variance (CV) reported in the previous literature'; <92% of baseline counted as fatigued; n = 9/14.
Garrett p.10: 'SWC was calculated as 0.2 x SD.'
Garrett p.6: 'average of six CMJs used for analysis'.
Ryan 2019 p.1-2: same-day retest in 18 players, test CV 6.3% above SWC 5.0%, and 'changes that exceed the CV (6.3%) are more meaningful than the SWC'. The claim correctly marks it as not a CMJ.
Parry p.2-3 quoted accurately, with 10 male college athletes and the upper-body test stated. The 8-9% applies to CMPU force.
Dos'Santos abstract: fixed bias in 6/16 and proportional bias in 10/16, with 2 male recreational soccer players.
Pommerell abstract and methods: 17 CrossFit athletes (3 women), four depths, quadratic relationship with an individual optimum.
Ryan 2020 Table 3 (p.4): n = 18, CV% 3.9/2.1/7.0/3.5/2.6 matched to the right variables.

Table 1 (p.2): n = 206, 35 players, weekly CV and SNR values and ratings all match. The source itself rates relative peak power 'Good' at SNR 1.5 but jump height 'Acceptable' at 1.5, and the claim reproduces this faithfully.
Statistics p.4 and conclusions p.5 match.

The claim splices two passages. The 'difficult to determine causes' sentence (p.5, left column) refers to the weekly testing approach not being fully rested. The 'not completely rested ... true reliability' sentence refers to the test-retest data. The joined meaning is close, so this does not change a decision.
p.5: 'did not relate these monitoring data against outcome measures (ie, injury or performance)'.
Collings p.6-7, p.9: 16 students (10 men, 6 women), physically active, about 7 days apart at the same time of day, ICC2,k with k = mean of 3.
Table 1 (p.21): CMJ height (Imp-Mom) 34 (7) and 34 (8), ICC 0.97, SEM 1.2, MDC 3.4. The footnote 'Based on the mean of 3 trials' is on p.23.
Conclusion p.15 and intro p.5 quoted accurately.
Garrett Table 5 (p.25): CMJ height TE 8.5% (7.1-10.8), SWC 1%. GymAware 'optical encoder' (p.7). p.11 says 'small CV', and p.15 concludes no variable could detect practically important changes.
Dos'Santos p.4: JH, RSImod and depth show no fixed or proportional bias at 1.0-1.7%, and 'practitioners are still advised to standardize'.
Pommerell p.2 (one jump per condition) and p.5: '9 cm ... led to a mean decrease of 0.6 ± 2.0 cm in hmax'.
Harper p.3, p.5-6: December mid-season, CMJ in the final session, five jumps 20 s apart, best and worst removed, remaining three averaged.
Ryan 2020 p.2 intro attributes the 1.1-7.1% range to ref 20, and the claim marks it as cited earlier research.

statementIssues.note: Calls the Garrett device a 'linear encoder', but the source and the rest of the brief say 'optical encoder'. It also labels the Harper 2.9% as 'within one session' although the paper does not say how that CV was derived (the limitations admit this).
'Only the student validation study retested on separate days' holds for the CMJ sources, but the cited push-up study (749) also retested 7 days apart. Wording should say 'only CMJ source'.
Says the AF authors 'attribute the difference to field versus laboratory testing', but the source hedges ('may be explained by'). C6 keeps the hedge.

The labeled professional judgment (a large depth change may partly explain a jump-height change) sits awkwardly next to the cited finding that a 9 cm deviation cost only 0.6 ± 2.0 cm, well below the 3.4 cm MDC. Labeled, so not critical.

'Do not compare across systems as if interchangeable' is somewhat stronger than 477, which found no bias for jump height, RSImod or depth (≤1.7%) and judged the system a valid alternative. It is still backed by the authors' advice to standardize systems and by Collings on analysis differences.

tierNote: Moderate is defensible for a methodological question. Sources agree on the change-versus-noise method, and two ForceDecks studies give explicit CMJ noise and SNR/MDC. Magnitude varies and transferability to collegiate in-season between-day testing is indirect, both stated openly. The tier is not Higher, so magnitude tension does not breach gating, and a conditional recommendation is allowed at Moderate.
usefulnessNote: Directly actionable for a sports scientist: estimate local TE/SEM, use MDC for 95% confidence, prefer metrics with high SNR, keep system and protocol constant. Numbers are traceable and transferability limits are honest. It is long, and the many reference values and side sources (push-up, adductor, CrossFit) slow a two-minute read. A clearer single worked example (for example, how many repeat sessions or athletes to estimate local TE) would raise it to a 5, but the library lacks that evidence and the brief lists it as a coverage gap.
suggestedDrafterFixes: Use one device descriptor per source across all statements, copied from the source's own wording, to avoid conflicts like linear vs optical encoder.
When a statement generalizes across sources ('only X did Y'), check it against every cited source, including non-target-test supporting studies, or scope it explicitly ('only CMJ source').
Carry the source's hedging verbs (may, suggest) from claims into synthesis statements such as evidenceTension.

When a statement says how a value was derived (for example 'within one session'), require a claim that states the derivation. Otherwise phrase it as 'from a single-session protocol; derivation not described'.
Flag labeled professional judgments that the adjacent cited data weakens, and either drop them or note the tension.
